items.title: Verdict convicting M Geethanandan, others in Muthanga land agitation case needs scrutiny: Kerala HC
items.summary: The Kerala High Court on Thursday observed that the conviction of four persons in a case arising from the 2003 Muthanga land struggle will require thorough scrutiny. Justice A Badharudeen made the observation after noting that the trial court's finding on the applicability of criminal conspiracy under Section 120B of the IPC was only prima facie in nature, and not conclusive. The Court was hearing appeals filed by activist M Geethanandan, and Rameshan, Binu and Anilkumar who were convicted by a sessions court over the violent confrontation between police and adivasi protesters at Muthanga in 2003. "The judgment needs to be scrutinised because the sessions judge made only a prima facie finding on the evidence... It should have been a conclusive finding. This judgment must be scrutinised thoroughly," the Court said in its order. The Muthanga land struggle stemmed from an eviction drive carried out by the Kerala Police at the Muthanga Wildlife Sanctuary in Wayanad in 2003. The eviction drive led to a violent confrontation between the police and Adivasi protesters, which escalated into police firing. Five protesters and police constable KV Vinod died in the incident. items.title: NLSIR reveals theme for inaugural Chief Justice ES Venkataramiah Memorial Best Essay Prize
items.summary: National Law School of India Review (NLSIR) has announced the theme for the inaugural edition of the Chief Justice ES Venkataramiah Memorial Best Essay Prize. The theme for this inaugural edition has now been announced as Does the Constitution Choose an Economic Model? Directive Principles and the Question of Ideological Neutrality. The theme draws on the Supreme Court's 2024 nine-judge Bench ruling in Property Owners' Association v. State of Maharashtra . The Bench had considered whether all privately owned property falls within the expression "material resources of the community" under Article 39(b) of the Constitution, a Directive Principle that asks the State to distribute the community's resources for the common good. The majority, led by then Chief Justice DY Chandrachud , held that it does not, reasoning that the Constitution does not commit India to a single economic ideology, and that treating all private property as a material resource would require the Court to endorse one particular vision of the country's economic and social order. In an affidavit filed before the top court, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment also said that the creamy layer principle cannot be applied to SC/STs and that only parliament can alter the lists of communities classified as SC/STs. Hence, the plea is misconceived and ought to be dismissed with exemplary costs, it was submitted. On the issue of whether the creamy layer concept, used to exclude the financially well placed among OBCs, could be extended to SC/STs as well, the government relied on the nine judge bench ruling in Indra Sawhney case to reject the suggestion. It was pointed out that the discussion on excluding the socially advanced in that judgment was expressly "confined to OBCs only and has no relevance in the case of SC/STs." The government further submitted that a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Ashoka Kumar Thakur judgment had clarified that for the purpose of reservation, the principles of creamy layer are not applicable to SC/ STs.
